title: Reverse a String
description: Brute force to optimized: building a reversed copy in a new array versus swapping in place with two pointers.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of characters s, reverse it so the elements end up in the opposite order, and do this in place, modifying the original array directly rather than returning a new one.

blocks.text: Given an array of characters s, reverse it so the elements end up in the opposite order, and do this in place, modifying the original array directly rather than returning a new one.

blocks.title: Analogy: Flipping a Line of People
blocks.text: Picture a line of people standing shoulder to shoulder, and imagine the person at the very front swapping places with the person at the very back, then the second person swapping with the second to last, and so on, working inward. By the time the two ends of the line meet in the middle, the whole line has been flipped, without ever needing a second line to stand in.

blocks.caption: Reverse the array in place, without creating a second array

blocks.text: An array with just one character is already its own reverse, nothing needs to change.
This problem sits right next to Valid Palindrome in the sheet for a reason, it is worth checking exactly how much of that earlier two pointer idea carries over directly.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Reversing an array in place and checking whether an array is a palindrome both rely on the exact same structural idea, work inward from both ends of the sequence at once.

Observation 2: The explicit in place requirement is a strong signal on its own, whenever a problem insists on no extra array, converging pointers from both ends is usually how that gets achieved.

Observation 3: This problem is actually simpler than Valid Palindrome, there is no filtering or skipping needed here, every position matters and every position gets touched exactly once.

Observation 4: Instead of comparing the two ends like Valid Palindrome did, this problem swaps them, exchanging the values at the two positions directly, then moving both pointers one step inward.

Recognizing this as the same converging two pointer structure as the symmetry check solved just before it, just swapping instead of comparing, is what makes the optimal solution obvious rather than something to search for from scratch.
Create a brand new array, walk through the original array from its last position back to its first, filling the new array in that order, then copy the new array's values back over the original.

items: Create a new array of the same length.
For every position i, copy the character from position n minus 1 minus i in the original into position i of the new array.
Copy every value from the new array back into the original array.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: build a reversed copy in a new array, then copy it back

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The reversed array is built as a completely separate structure first, so that the original array is never read from and written to at the same time during that first pass.
A second, explicit pass copies every value back into the original array, since the problem requires the original array itself to end up reversed, not just a new array elsewhere.
Both passes are simple, single direction loops, one filling the new array back to front, and one copying it forward, with no conditional logic needed since every position always participates.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every position in the new array is filled directly from the mirrored position in the original.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to fill the new array, and another pass to copy it back.
Space: O(n), for the entire extra array.

Limitation: the problem only asks for the array to be reversed in place, so building a whole second array of the same size is unnecessary. Two values that need to swap positions can simply be exchanged directly, without any extra storage beyond the two positions involved.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why building a reversed copy works but is wasteful: it stores every value a second time, in a whole new array, purely to move each one to its mirrored position.

What actually needs to happen to each pair of positions: the values at position i and position n minus 1 minus i simply need to trade places with each other.

Can that trade happen without any extra storage beyond the two positions themselves: yes, a direct swap exchanges two values using only a small, constant amount of temporary space, not an entire second array.

Can this be applied to every pair at once, working inward: yes, starting one pointer at each end and moving both inward after every swap touches every pair exactly once.

The core idea: two pointers, one at each end, swap their values directly and move inward until they meet, using no extra array at all.

Use two pointers, one starting at the first position and one at the last. Swap the characters at those two positions directly, then move both pointers one step inward. Repeat until the pointers meet or cross, at which point the entire array has been reversed.
Two pointers start at opposite ends of the array, swap their values directly, then move one step inward, repeating until they meet.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: swap the two ends directly and move both pointers inward

blocks.text: This works because reversing an array is exactly a collection of independent pairwise swaps, the value that belongs at position i is exactly the value that started at position n minus 1 minus i, and vice versa. Swapping those two positions directly places both values exactly where they need to end up, and doing this for every pair from the outside in, until the two pointers meet or cross, touches every position exactly once with no position ever revisited.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each pair of positions is swapped exactly once.
Space: O(1) extra space, this is the real floor for this problem, since every position must still be touched at least once, but no extra array is ever needed.

blocks.text: Reversing a sequence in place is one of the clearest examples of the two pointer pattern, working inward from both ends at once avoids the extra memory of a second copy entirely, turning an O(n) space solution into an O(1) space one while keeping the same O(n) time.

items: Continuing to swap after the two pointers have already met or crossed, which would undo the reversal for the middle elements.
Returning a new array instead of modifying the given one in place, when the problem specifically asks for an in place reversal.
Off by one errors in the starting position of the right pointer, it should start at the last valid index, not the length itself.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Empty array or a single character array","Both are already their own reverse, nothing needs to change."],["An array with an odd number of elements","The single middle element never needs to move."]]}

blocks.text: Recognizing that an in place requirement is a strong hint toward the two pointer pattern, rather than building any auxiliary structure, is one of the fastest ways to spot the intended optimal solution for this style of problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this in place", think: two pointers starting at each end, swapping directly and moving inward.
If the interviewer says "how is this related to Valid Palindrome", think: the same converging two pointer structure, swapping instead of comparing.
If the interviewer says "what about the middle element", think: the loop condition naturally stops before the pointers cross, leaving a lone middle element untouched.

items: Why does an explicit in place requirement so often point directly at the two pointer pattern?
How would you reverse only a specific window or substring within a larger array, rather than the whole thing?
Can you reverse the array using recursion instead of an explicit loop, and what would that cost in extra space?
How would this approach change if the array were a singly linked list instead of a plain array?
How would you reverse the words in a sentence while keeping the letters within each word in their original order?
Valid Palindrome, which uses this exact same converging two pointer structure to compare instead of swap.
Any in place array transformation, where a strong hint toward two pointers is the explicit requirement to avoid extra memory.
Rotate Array and similar problems, which often use multiple reversal passes, each built from this same swap-in-place technique, to achieve an in place rotation.
Reverse Linked List, which reuses the same "flip from both directions" intuition but with pointer rewiring instead of array index swaps.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force approach runs in O(n) time and O(n) extra space, needing a full second array. The two pointer approach also runs in O(n) time but only O(1) extra space, the real floor for this problem, since every position must be visited at least once to reverse it.

items: Pattern: two pointers converging from both ends of a sequence, swapping in place instead of building a reversed copy.

Core Idea: the value that belongs at position i is exactly the value that started at position n minus 1 minus i, so swapping those two positions directly, working inward from both ends, reverses the whole array with no extra storage.
Time: O(n) for both the brute force and the optimized version.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, to hold the entire reversed copy; O(1) extra for the optimized two pointer version.
Most Important Observation: an explicit in place requirement is one of the strongest possible hints toward the two pointer swap pattern.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the brute force version; immediately reaching for two pointers because of the in place requirement is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: two pointers, swap directly, move inward until they meet.
